title: Titanic Birth Records
subtitle: Fictional 1912 birth records for the Titanic's passengers — eight archive shapes
description:
A fictional but historically careful reconstruction of birth
records for the passengers of the Titanic — the classic
`titanic.csv` manifest joined to the mess it could have come
from.

**`titanic-birth-records.json`** holds 1,146 records across
eight registration systems of 1912, each with its own tree
shape: GRO quarterly indexes, Irish parish registers, Swedish
kyrkoböcker, French actes de naissance, US state records,
Ottoman nüfus, Latin matricula baptizatorum, and Russian
metricheskie knigi (Julian dates included). Names are spelled
the way each system would spell them, ages disagree the way
archives disagree, and some passengers simply are not there —
the coverage gaps are part of the data.

The set is **deterministically generated**:
`gen-titanic-birth-records.py` (seeded) rebuilds the JSON
byte-identically from the included classic tables
(`titanic.csv`, `test.csv`, `titanic3.csv`). Two executed
companion notebooks walk the exploration end to end, and
`births.quarb` carries reusable query fragments.

It accompanies the article
[The rest of the iceberg](https://quarb.org/articles/the-rest-of-the-iceberg.html)
(joining, anti-joining, and age recovery across all eight
shapes with [Quarb](https://quarb.org)); the source repo is
[github.com/deyanovich/titanic-birth-records](https://github.com/deyanovich/titanic-birth-records).

## Provenance & methodology

**Sources.** The three manifest tables are the public-domain
classics: Kaggle's train/test split (`titanic.csv`,
`test.csv`) and the full `titanic3` table of the
Vanderbilt/Encyclopedia-Titanica lineage. The birth records
are **fictional**, generated from those tables.

**Methodology.** `gen-titanic-birth-records.py` is seeded and
deterministic: every archive shape, spelling rule, calendar
system, disagreement, and coverage gap is an explicit,
reviewable rule in the generator — re-run it and the JSON
rebuilds byte-identically. Column-level documentation lives on
each file's schema here; the full walkthrough is the companion
article and the two attached notebooks.

**Update cadence.** The dataset is complete as designed;
versions only follow generator refinements (never silent data
churn).

resources.description: The classic Kaggle train split: 891 passengers, 12 columns, byte-for-byte the table everyone has modeled — here it plays the tip of the iceberg that the birth records sit under.

fields.name: PassengerId
fields.description: Row id, 1–891 — the classic Kaggle train split. The birth records cite this id from every archive (1,146 citations across ids 1–1309).

fields.name: Survived
fields.description: 1 = survived, 0 = did not. Present only in this file; the birth records deliberately carry no survival information (no leakage).

fields.name: Pclass
fields.description: Ticket class (1, 2, 3) — the usual proxy for socio-economic standing.

fields.name: Name
fields.description: Full name as the manifest spells it: 'Surname, Title. Given (Maiden)' — married women appear under husbands' names with maiden names in parentheses; the archives spell the same people their own ways.

fields.name: Sex
fields.description: male / female, as recorded.

fields.name: Age
fields.description: Age in years at sailing, as the manifest recorded it — fractional for infants (0.92 = 11 months), blank where the manifest is silent; the birth records exist to fill and cross-examine exactly those blanks.

fields.name: SibSp
fields.description: Siblings + spouses aboard. The birth-record patronymics and parish sibling entries corroborate (or complicate) these counts.

fields.name: Parch
fields.description: Parents + children aboard.

fields.name: Ticket
fields.description: Ticket number, as printed.

fields.name: Fare
fields.description: Fare paid, pounds sterling.

fields.name: Cabin
fields.description: Cabin number where known; mostly blank in third class.

fields.name: Embarked
fields.description: Port of embarkation: C = Cherbourg, Q = Queenstown, S = Southampton.

resources.description: The dataset proper: 1,146 fictional birth records across eight 1912 registration systems, each with its own authentic tree shape — GRO quarterly index (England & Wales), Irish civil registration, Swedish kyrkoböcker, French actes de naissance, US state vital records, Ottoman nüfus (Rumi years), Latin matricula baptizatorum, Russian metricheskie knigi (Julian dates). Every record cites a passenger_id; names, dates, and precisions disagree exactly the way real archives disagree, and the coverage gaps are deliberate. No survival information anywhere.

The seeded, deterministic generator: rebuilds titanic-birth-records.json byte-identically from the three CSV tables. Reading it is reading the dataset's complete methodology — every disagreement, misspelling, and gap is a documented rule, not noise.
A commented Quarb fragment library for querying the records — the calendar conversions (Julian, Rumi) and per-archive year extraction used by the companion article and notebooks.
The dataset card: what each archive shape looks like, the join keys, the no-leakage rules (no survival information in the records), and links to the companion article and notebooks.
